The Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Professor Muhammad Ali Pate, who stated this on Thursday in Kaduna, warned that strengthening the nursing workforce remains critical to improving healthcare delivery.
He stressed the need for sustained investment in nursing education, professional development and improved working conditions.
Pate, represented by the Director of Nursing in the ministry, Mrs Imaobong Umar, spoke at the launch and public presentation of a book titled: “A Compendium of the Struggles for the Establishment of Nursing Science Degree in Northern Nigeria,” authored by retired nurse, Alhaji Dr Mustapha Jumare.
“The federal government recognises that a strong health system cannot exist without a well-protected, adequately trained, motivated, and appropriately distributed nursing force,” he said.
The minister said the government was working with regulatory bodies, academic institutions, professional associations and development partners to strengthen nursing education and professional development.
He, however, cautioned that the expansion of university-based nursing education must be accompanied by stronger alternative nursing education pathways, adequate clinical training opportunities and strict adherence to professional standards.
“Our ultimate goal is to produce nurses who are not only academically qualified but also clinically competent, ethically grounded, evidence-informed, and capable of providing compassionate, patient-centred care,” he said.
Pate identified nurses as central to achieving universal health coverage, noting that they constitute the first point of contact between patients, families and the healthcare system, particularly at the primary healthcare level.
He noted that nurses provide essential services, including health promotion, disease prevention, early diagnosis and treatment, maternal and child healthcare, as well as newborn care.
The minister also called for expanded leadership opportunities for nurses, insisting that their expertise must be recognised in health policy development, planning, implementation, monitoring and evaluation.
Earlier, Kaduna State Deputy Governor, Dr Hadiza Balarabe, described the book as an important historical account of the sacrifices and institutional struggles that led to the establishment of nursing degree programmes in Northern Nigeria.
Representing Governor Uba Sani, she said, “Some struggles are too important to be forgotten and some victories are too significant to be left undocumented.”
She commended Jumare for preserving the contributions of pioneers of nursing education in the region, describing the publication as a valuable resource for students, educators, policymakers and future healthcare professionals.
The founder of Maryam Abacha American University, Professor Adamu Abubakar Gwarzo, who was the chief launcher, described nursing science as a highly employable degree, citing the employment of the university’s graduates in the United States, Thailand, Saudi Arabia and the United Kingdom.
He, therefore, commended the author for documenting the struggle to establish Bachelor of Nursing Science degree programmes in Northern Nigeria.
The chairman of the Central Planning Committee for the book launch, Alheri Grace Yusuf, a nurse, described the publication as a significant record of the struggles and sacrifices that preceded the establishment of nursing education in Northern Nigeria.
Yusuf said before the establishment of the nursing department in the region, aspiring nurses had to travel to Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife, Osun State, or the University of Ibadan, Oyo State, to obtain degree qualifications.
She said the distance and family responsibilities made it difficult for many nurses, particularly married women, to pursue university education outside the region.
She said, “With our culture, you can’t leave your husband and children and travel to go and spend three years in the name of studies. So, the need was really serious.”
According to her, the advocacy led by Jumare and other pioneers was instrumental in securing the establishment of the nursing department, providing greater access to degree-level nursing education in the region.
She said the book had preserved the records of the correspondence, official memoranda and various efforts that culminated in the establishment of the programme.
“For us, for someone to keep records of all the processes, the steps, the memos and the ups and downs that were involved in ensuring that the department was established is a great achievement,” she said.
Yusuf added that the occasion was not just a book launch but a celebration of resilience, goodwill and the importance of preserving institutional history.
She disclosed that, according to records presented to the committee, the programme had graduated close to 10,000 nurses so far after it started in Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria.
A co-launcher from the United States of America, Alhaji Garba Suleiman, commended the author for his doggedness in documenting the struggle, asking universities, nursing colleges, hospitals among others, to have copies of the book in their archives.
